title: Universal tuning of Förster resonance energy transfer in gate-programmable conductor-dielectric-conductor heterostructures
authors: Alexis J. Agosto, Daniel Gunlycke, Michael N. Leuenberger
abstract: We develop a quantum-electrodynamical theory for universal tuning of spontaneous emission and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) in a material-agnostic conductor-dielectric-conductor heterostructure. The platform consists of a dielectric spacer of thickness $W$ bounded by two gate-tunable two-dimensional conductors. The only microscopic input from the surrounding materials is the transverse-magnetic and transverse-electric reflection amplitudes $r_{\TM/\TE}(q_ρ,ω)$ of the two sheets. Starting from the QED photon propagator, we derive the retarded Maxwell dyadic, the vacuum/Hadamard field propagator, and the time-ordered Feynman propagator in the same geometry. The spontaneous-emission rate is controlled by the local vacuum spectral density, while FRET is controlled by the nonlocal retarded/advanced product $\obG_{\text R}(\bx_D,\bx_A;ω_D)\Im\,\balpha_A(ω_D)\obG_{\text A}(\bx_A,\bx_D;ω_D)$. In the transparent limit $r_{\TM}\to 0$, the near-field FRET rate recovers the bulk $x_ρ^{-6}$ law. In the Dirichlet/PEC branch $r_{\TM}\to -1$, the gapless transverse mode is removed and the donor-acceptor coupling acquires a Bessel-$K$ envelope, giving an exponentially screened FRET rate $Γ_{D\to A}\propto\exp(-2πx_ρ/W)$ at large lateral separation. In the opposite Neumann/PMC-like branch $r_{\TM}\to 1^{-}$, a nearly gapless transverse mode survives and produces a wide quasi-two-dimensional logarithmic propagator, enhancing the nonlocal electromagnetic coupling over a gate-programmable range $x_{ρ,*}\sim W/(1-r_{\TM})$. For graphene-Er implementations, the same retarded Green tensor also separates dissipative on-shell Er-to-graphene decay, governed by its absorptive part, from dispersive virtual-plasmon-mediated Er-Er coupling, governed by its reactive part; a plasmonic band gap can suppress the former while retaining the latter.
summary: This paper presents a quantum electrodynamics theory for controlling energy transfer (FRET) and spontaneous emission in structures defined by two gate-tunable conductors separated by a dielectric spacer. By analyzing the system's response via reflection amplitudes, the authors show that the coupling can be tuned from bulk decay laws to exponentially screened or enhanced quasi-2D regimes. This offers a versatile platform for manipulating quantum light-matter interactions using electrical gating.
main_problem: The paper develops a quantum-electrodynamical theory to universally tune spontaneous emission and Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) in a specific heterostructure.
main_result: The theory predicts distinct coupling regimes based on gate-tunable reflection amplitudes, ranging from bulk decay laws to exponentially screened or enhanced quasi-2D couplings.
method: The authors derive the necessary Green's functions (retarded, advanced, Feynman) starting from the QED photon propagator and analyze the system's response using reflection amplitudes.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a conductor-dielectric-conductor heterostructure with a dielectric spacer of thickness W, bounded by two gate-tunable two-dimensional conductors (e.g., graphene).
key_observables: Spontaneous emission rate (via local vacuum spectral density) and FRET rate (via nonlocal retarded/advanced Green tensor product).
important_parameters: Dielectric spacer thickness (W), lateral separation ($x_ho$), and the gate-tunable reflection amplitudes ($r_{TM/TE}$).
main_assumptions: The theory relies on the input reflection amplitudes $r_{TM/TE}(q_ho, \omega)$ from the surrounding materials, and the analysis is performed in the quasi-2D limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how gate tuning modifies reflection amplitudes, thereby reprogramming the range and magnitude of the donor–acceptor electromagnetic coupling, and show the separation of dissipative vs. dispersive coupling components.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by deriving propagators from the QED photon propagator, analyzing the system response in different reflection regimes (transparent, PEC, PMC-like), and applying the formalism to specific material systems like graphene-Er.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, material-agnostic theoretical framework for controlling near-field quantum interactions (like FRET) using external electrical gates, which is highly relevant to cavity QED and open quantum systems.
